subtopic: Found money or a lost wallet
subtype: Approach: pros and cons of keeping it [Thinking]
passage: In the corridor after school I saw Yash pick up a folded wad of notes. He sat on the steps, took out his rough notebook, and I peeked. Two columns. Under KEEP: cricket bat. Under GIVE BACK: what if they are counting on it for the doctor, or the flat's rent? And below that, in small letters: I will remember it every time I swing. He chewed his pencil for a long time. I can't tell whether he was more tempted or more scared. Then he stood up, walked to the office, and Hansa Ma'am, the clerk, took the notes and wrote his name in the register. - Mahima

qa.q: What did Yash write under KEEP?
What might Yash have been feeling while he chewed his pencil?
qa.a: Torn between temptation and guilt, though Mahima cannot be sure which feeling was stronger.

qa.q: What other approach could Yash use to decide, and why?
qa.a: He could ask a parent or teacher what they would do, or imagine the money was his own, which makes the owner's need easier to feel.

qa.q: How does Mahima see Yash's decision?
qa.a: Mahima cannot tell what Yash felt, but sees him walk to the office and treats it as a thoughtful choice.

grounding: A boy weighs keeping the found money against the owner's possible needs and his own guilt before deciding.

subtopic: Found money or a lost wallet
subtype: Approach: pros and cons of keeping it [Thinking]
passage:
Friday: Kamal found a purse in the lane with eight hundred rupees in it. His heart raced. He hid it under his mattress.
Saturday: He tore a page from his notebook and drew two columns. KEEP: a new cricket bat, the one with the red grip. GIVE BACK: the owner could need it for medicine. Maybe it's their rent. He paused. Then he added one more line under KEEP: I would feel bad every time I held the bat. He looked at the page for a long time. The GIVE BACK side felt heavier.
Sunday: He showed his sister Nandini the list and the purse. She went with him to their mother, who took it to the shop where the owner had put up a notice.

qa.q: How much money was in the purse?
How did Kamal feel when he looked at the page for a long time?
qa.a: He felt torn between wanting the bat and feeling guilty, and the guilt started to weigh more.

qa.q: What else could Kamal do next time he finds something, and why?
qa.a: He could tell an adult straight away instead of hiding it, so there is less time for temptation and worry.

qa.q: How does Kamal's decision look to Nandini?
qa.a: Nandini sees her brother choose honesty after thinking hard, and supports him by going with him to their mother.

grounding: It shows a child listing that keeping found money buys a cricket bat but the owner might need it for medicine or rent, and that he would feel guilty.

subtopic: Found money or a lost wallet
subtype: Approach: pros and cons of keeping it [Thinking]
passage: Dilnaz, you found ten rupees and want to buy sweets? Let your Jomon Uncle tell you about a purse I found when I was a boy. It was on the church steps, with a few hundred rupees in it. That was a lot of money then. I wanted a real cricket bat so badly. I sat under the mango tree and argued with myself. Keep it: bat. Give it: maybe the money was someone's medicine. Maybe it was for the school fees of some child like me. And every time I swung that bat, I'd remember. I would never enjoy it. So I gave it to the priest. An old woman came the next day, crying. It was her pension.

qa.q: Where did young Jomon find the purse?
How did young Jomon feel while arguing with himself under the mango tree?
qa.a: Young Jomon felt torn and tempted, wanting the bat but also uneasy and guilty about keeping it.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and what else could Jomon have done?
qa.a: Imagining that every swing of the bat would bring back the memory was the turning point; Jomon could also have asked a parent to help find the owner.

qa.q: How might the old woman have felt when she got her purse back?
qa.a: She would have felt deep relief and gratitude, since it was her pension.

grounding: An elder recalls, as a boy, weighing a cricket bat against the owner's possible need and his own guilt, and returning a found purse.
